notes: Shearer's JLP holds ruling slot 1. Jamaica has no real coalition partner; template slot 2 is filled with the Jamaica Council for Human Rights (liberal civil-liberties body). PNP placed in slot 3 (MD uses 18, which has no starting popularity); its union NWU goes to 18. Rastafari in 6 (anti-Babylon traditionalism), Abeng Black Power in 5, Rodney's Groundings in 19, Seaga's Tivoli garrison in 0, BITU in 14, House of Windsor in 23.

0.name: Tivoli Gardens
0.text:
Tivoli Gardens is the housing scheme built in West Kingston on the bulldozed ruins of the Back-o-Wall shantytown and the stronghold of Edward Seaga, the JLP member for the constituency and Minister of Finance and Planning since 1967. Its residents receive homes, jobs and protection in exchange for unbending loyalty, enforced by party gunmen.

The Tivoli model stands for firm, centralized, pro-American rule: anti-communism, private enterprise, state patronage and the street power to defeat the PNP by any means. Its base is the party's urban poor, contractors and enforcers. Its leverage lies in votes delivered en bloc and in men ready to fight for them.

1.name: Jamaica Labour Party
1.text:
The Jamaica Labour Party was founded in 1943 by Alexander Bustamante as the political arm of his Bustamante Industrial Trade Union and led the island to independence in 1962. Since Donald Sangster's death in 1967 it has been led by Prime Minister Hugh Shearer, who governs with the majority won in the February 1967 election.

The JLP stands for capitalist development led by bauxite, tourism and manufacturing, firm alignment with the United States and Britain, and anti-communism. Its government banned Black Power literature and excluded the historian Walter Rodney in 1968. Its base is the BITU, rural farmers, business and the party's urban strongholds in Kingston.

2.name: Jamaica Council for Human Rights
2.text:
The Jamaica Council for Human Rights was formed in 1968 by lawyers, clergymen and academics alarmed at police brutality, prison conditions and the Shearer government's response to the Rodney riots of October 1968, including bans on books and travel restrictions on radicals. It acts as a watchdog rather than a party.

Its members stand for civil liberties, the rule of law, free speech, an independent judiciary and constitutional government in the Westminster tradition, and are firmly Western in outlook. Its supporters are middle-class professionals, journalists and university staff. Its leverage lies in the courts, the press and appeals to Commonwealth opinion.

3.name: People's National Party
3.text:
The People's National Party was founded in 1938 by Norman Manley and governed Jamaica in the 1950s before losing the 1962 and 1967 elections. In February 1969 Michael Manley, the founder's son and a former leading figure of the National Workers' Union, succeeded his father as party president and leader of the opposition.

The PNP calls itself democratic socialist: it seeks greater social justice, land reform, workers' participation, equal pay and a more independent foreign policy, while remaining within the Western camp. It is courting Black Power-minded youth and the urban poor. Its base is the NWU, professionals, teachers and the Kingston constituencies its activists control.

4.name: The Mona Marxists
4.text:
The Mona Marxists are study groups of lecturers and students at the University of the West Indies campus at Mona, joined by a few veterans of the communist left expelled from the PNP in 1952. Since the exclusion of Walter Rodney in 1968, Special Branch watches them closely, and their literature is often seized at the ports.

They look to the Soviet Union and Cuba, calling for a vanguard party of workers and peasants, nationalization of the bauxite and sugar industries and an end to dependence on Britain and the United States. Their base is the campus, a few union militants and readers of radical journals. Their leverage lies in ideas and in training future cadres.

5.name: Abeng
5.text:
Abeng is the Black Power movement that grew around the weekly newspaper of that name, launched in February 1969 after the Rodney riots by university radicals including George Beckford, Robert Hill and Rupert Lewis. Named after the horn of the Maroons, it brought together Rastafari, trade unionists, students and the unemployed before the paper ceased publication later that year.

Abeng demands Black economic power, an end to foreign ownership of land and bauxite, the dismantling of the colonial social order and solidarity with Africa and the Third World. It distrusts both parties as instruments of the elite. Its leverage lies in the radicalized youth of Kingston.

6.name: Rastafari movement
6.text:
The Rastafari movement emerged in the 1930s from the preaching of Leonard Howell and others who hailed Emperor Haile Selassie I of Ethiopia as the returned messiah. Long persecuted, its brethren won new respect when the emperor visited Kingston in 1966; elders such as Mortimo Planno speak for the yards of West Kingston, and the Twelve Tribes of Israel was founded in 1968.

Rastafari rejects Babylon, the Western colonial system with its police and its politics, and calls for repatriation to Africa, Black dignity and a natural way of life. Its base is the urban poor and artists. Its leverage is cultural, through music and moral authority.

7.name: Special Branch of the Jamaica Constabulary Force
7.english: Special Branch of the Jamaica Constabulary Force
7.text:
The Special Branch is the political intelligence unit of the Jamaica Constabulary Force, built on British colonial models and strengthened after the Rodney riots of October 1968. It monitors Black Power groups, Rastafari, university radicals and trade union militants, compiles banned lists and advises the Ministry of Home Affairs on exclusions and restrictions.

As a power bloc it stands for permanent vigilance against subversion, sweeping powers of search and detention and censorship of dangerous literature. It works closely with British and American intelligence. Its leverage lies in its files, its informers and the government's fear of unrest in the Kingston slums.

8.name: Hosay
8.text:
Hosay is the Muharram festival brought to Jamaica by Indian indentured labourers in the nineteenth century, commemorating the martyrdom of Imam Husayn with decorated tadjahs and drumming in Clarendon and Westmoreland. The committees that organize it keep alive a Shia devotional heritage among Indo-Jamaicans, though Hindus and Afro-Jamaicans now join the processions.

The committees stand for religious freedom, community pride and the preservation of Indian traditions in a nation whose motto is Out of Many, One People. They seek a modest renewal of Muslim learning and contact with Shia centres abroad. Their influence lies in rural Indian communities and the sugar estates.

9.name: Disciples of Najaf
9.text:
The Disciples of Najaf are a few young Indo-Jamaican Muslims and Caribbean students in London who have encountered revolutionary Shia literature from Iraq, where the exiled Iranian Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini has taught since 1965. They correspond with seminarians and hold occasional gatherings in Kingston homes.

They argue that the learned clergy must guide the faithful against tyranny and imperialism, and read Jamaica's colonial past in that light. Dismissing the folk traditions of Hosay as diluted, they want a disciplined, scholarly Shia faith. Without institutions or numbers, their leverage is negligible.

10.name: The Spanish Town Jamaat
10.text:
The Spanish Town Jamaat is a small Sunni congregation of Indo-Jamaican descendants of indentured labourers and a few Arab traders, meeting in Spanish Town and the sugar parishes. It receives Korans, teachers and literature from the Muslim World League, founded in Mecca in 1962.

It preaches quietist orthodoxy: correct worship, Arabic learning, obedience to lawful authority and rejection of folk accretions such as Hosay drumming. It is anti-communist and looks to Saudi Arabia for guidance and funds, while seeking official recognition of Muslim marriages and holidays. Its leverage lies in scholarships and Arab contacts.

11.name: The Khilafat Circle
11.text:
The Khilafat Circle is a handful of Jamaican students and converts who encountered Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Islamic Liberation Party founded in Jerusalem in 1953, while studying in London. Its name recalls the Khilafat movement of their Indian forebears. In Kingston they distribute duplicated tracts and debate at the Mona campus.

They denounce nationalism, Westminster democracy and both superpowers, and preach that only a restored caliphate can free Muslims and the colonized peoples. They seek converts among Black Power youth. Without numbers or resources, their leverage is confined to campus debate.

12.name: Kingston Black Muslims
12.text:
The Kingston Black Muslims are young Afro-Jamaicans drawn to Islam by the example of Malcolm X, assassinated in 1965, and by the Nation of Islam's newspaper Muhammad Speaks, brought home by migrants from New York and London. They meet in Kingston yards and debate with Rastafari and Black Power activists.

They preach discipline, self-reliance, Black economic independence and Islam as the original faith of Africans, rejecting the Christian churches as instruments of slavery. Increasingly drawn to orthodox Sunni teaching, as Malcolm X was, they reject both the JLP and the PNP. Their leverage lies in their appeal to the young urban poor.

13.name: Jamaica Industrial Development Corporation
13.text:
The Jamaica Industrial Development Corporation was established in 1952 to attract manufacturing investment through tax holidays, factory buildings and industrial estates. Together with the Central Planning Unit and a senior civil service trained in the British tradition, it forms the technocratic core of a state that has outlasted changes of government.

The planners favour industrialization by invitation, state-guided investment, infrastructure and stable labour relations, without strong commitment to either party or bloc. They value expertise over politics and distrust both garrison patronage and radical nationalization. Their leverage lies in development finance, administrative continuity and the confidence of foreign investors.

14.name: Bustamante Industrial Trade Union
14.text:
The Bustamante Industrial Trade Union was founded in 1938 by Alexander Bustamante in the wake of that year's labour rebellion and remains the largest union in Jamaica, strong among sugar workers, dockers and bauxite workers. Bustamante, retired from active politics, is still its revered chief, and Hugh Shearer rose through its ranks.

The BITU combines militant wage bargaining with loyalty to the JLP, the Crown, the churches and the Western camp, and it is fiercely anti-communist. Its members are rural workers and the island's conservative working class. Its leverage lies in its membership, its strike power and its role as the JLP's electoral backbone.

15.name: Jamaica Manufacturers' Association
15.text:
The Jamaica Manufacturers' Association, founded in 1947, speaks for the family conglomerates that grew rich behind tariff walls and industrial incentives, alongside the merchant houses, sugar interests and the North American bauxite and alumina companies that dominate the economy. A few interlinked families, such as the Matalons, sit on the boards of banks, insurers and newspapers.

The business elite backs the JLP's pro-investment policy, protection for local industry and labour peace, and fears the radical nationalism of Black Power. It finances both parties to be safe. Its leverage lies in capital, jobs, the media and direct access to ministers.

16.name: Jamaica Chamber of Commerce
16.text:
The Jamaica Chamber of Commerce, dating back to 1779, represents Kingston's import and distribution merchants, insurance agents and shopkeepers, the oldest organized business interest on the island. Its members chafe at import licensing, quotas and the tariffs that protect local manufacturers at the expense of consumers and traders.

The Chamber argues for free trade, low taxes, balanced budgets, sound money and minimal state interference, and sees opportunity in the Caribbean Free Trade Association that Jamaica joined in 1968. Firmly pro-Western, it distrusts both nationalization talk and political patronage. Its leverage lies in trade, credit and long-standing access to government.

17.name: Natural History Society of Jamaica
17.text:
The Natural History Society of Jamaica brings together naturalists, scientists of the Institute of Jamaica and the University of the West Indies, and amateur birdwatchers concerned about the island's vanishing forests, wetlands and endemic species. It publishes field studies and lobbies quietly for protection of the Blue Mountains and the Cockpit Country.

Its members call for national parks, watershed protection, controls on bauxite red mud and hillside clearing, and the preservation of coral reefs threatened by tourism development. They are politically neutral, middle-class and scientific in outlook. Their leverage lies in expert knowledge and the prestige of the Institute of Jamaica.

18.name: National Workers' Union
18.text:
The National Workers' Union was founded in 1952 after the PNP expelled its Marxist wing and broke with the Trades Union Congress, and it built its strength by winning recognition in the bauxite industry. Michael Manley made his name as its island supervisor and chief negotiator before entering politics; the union remains the PNP's industrial arm.

The NWU stands for workers' rights, higher wages, union recognition, worker participation in management and greater national control over bauxite. Non-communist but more radical than the BITU, it fuses labour militancy with nationalism. Its leverage lies in the mines, factories and docks it organizes.

19.name: Groundings
19.text:
Groundings takes its name from Walter Rodney's practice of grounding with Rastafari and the urban poor in the yards of Kingston, recorded in his book The Groundings with My Brothers, published in 1969. The Guyanese historian was barred from Jamaica in October 1968 and now teaches in Dar es Salaam, but circles of his disciples continue to meet.

They combine Marxism with Black Power and pan-Africanism, rejecting both the Soviet model and Westminster party politics, and seek a revolution rooted in African culture and the Third World. Their base is students, Rastafari and unemployed youth. Their leverage lies in ideas and in their bridge between campus and ghetto.

20.name: People's Political Party
20.text:
The People's Political Party was founded in 1961 by the lawyer Millard Johnson to carry forward the programme of Marcus Garvey, whose own party of the same name contested the elections of 1930. It fared poorly in the 1962 election and is largely dormant, but its slogans of Black pride and self-reliance echo through the Black Power upsurge.

The PPP rejects the brown and white elite and both major parties, and calls for Black ownership of land and business, national pride and moral discipline, honouring Garvey as a National Hero. Its base is the small Black middle class and the urban poor. Its leverage lies in Garvey's symbolic power.

21.name: The Iron Hand
21.text:
The Iron Hand is the hard-line faction of politicians, senior police officers, magistrates and newspaper columnists who answered the Rodney riots of October 1968 with demands for emergency powers, flogging and the banning of subversive literature. Some West Kingston party enforcers share its creed of force.

It calls for a strong state above parliamentary niceties: detention without trial for agitators, suppression of Black Power and Rastafari activism, exclusion of foreign radicals and harsh punishment for crime. Fiercely anti-communist and loyal to the Crown and the West, it draws on a frightened middle class. Its leverage lies in the police and the courts.

22.name: Jamaica Defence Force
22.text:
The Jamaica Defence Force was formed at independence in 1962 from the Jamaica Regiment of the former West Indies Federation, and remains small, British-trained and professional. It has been deployed alongside the police during the Kingston disturbances of recent years, including the Rodney riots of October 1968.

The officer corps is apolitical by tradition, loyal to the Crown and the constitution, and closely linked to the British Army through training at Sandhurst. It values discipline, order and Western alignment. Its leverage lies in being the ultimate guarantor of internal security should party violence or unrest overwhelm the police.

23.name: House of Windsor
23.text:
The House of Windsor reigns over Jamaica through Queen Elizabeth II, who remained head of state when the island became independent within the Commonwealth in 1962. Her representative, Governor-General Sir Clifford Campbell, the first Jamaican to hold the office, appoints the prime minister and gives assent to laws.

The Crown stands for constitutional continuity, the Westminster system, the Commonwealth link and ceremonial unity above party. Its supporters are the older generation, the churches, the civil service, the armed forces and much of the middle class. Its leverage is symbolic and constitutional, though Black Power and Rastafari voices increasingly question a British monarch's place.
